source.title: Asymptotic theory of in-context learning by linear attention
source.authors: Yue M. Lu; Mary I. Letey; Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth; Anindita Maiti; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study conceptually tests sample-wise double descent using synthetic in-context linear regression and Transformer models, rather than reproducing the original studies’ settings.
record.gate_note: The relevant results vary pretraining sample count and report test/generalization error curves. Context-length and task-diversity results are not rows because they do not test the listed versions. Interpolation-threshold scaling exponents are not rows because they measure threshold location, not test error. The cited findings of other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own sample-wise test-error curves in a new setting: in-context linear regression by linear attention, with theory plus simulation, and full Transformers. Error rises with more pretraining samples up to the interpolation threshold (n ≈ d², τ=1) and falls after it. This bears directly on V3. A ridge-strength comparison bears on the regularization part of V6. The record's T2 is defensible, but this is a new setting rather than a different method on the original setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the solvable linear-attention model shows sample-wise double descent, with the peak at the interpolation threshold (n ≈ d²), suppressed by ridge regularization. Full nonlinear Transformers show qualitatively similar behaviour, with thresholds scaling roughly as d². They caution that double descent in pretraining examples is unlikely to carry over to fully online training, because it reflects training to interpolation on a fixed dataset.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes pretraining on synthetic in-context linear-regression examples, using a ridge-regression reduction and separate Adam-trained Transformer experiments; it does not reproduce the original studies’ model-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The peak is suppressed by stronger ridge regularization. The authors report possible deviations near the peak for the full linear model and at large τ for the deep nonlinear model; they attribute these possibly to parameter inversion or instability and to the training procedure, respectively. The reduced-model non-monotonicity with context length depends on task diversity and noise, but that is not a test of the listed versions.

fits_no_version.finding: ICL and IDG error can be non-monotonic in context length α, with a finite optimal α*; ICL error diverges in α for κ ≤ min(τ,1) in the ridgeless limit (Figs. 2–3, Eq. 17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test error can be non-monotonic, and can even diverge, along the context-length axis in in-context learning, depending on task diversity and noise.

fits_no_version.finding: The empirical interpolation threshold, where the peak occurs, scales as n ∝ d^a with a ≈ 1.66–2.13 across Transformer architectures (Fig. 5d).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The sample-wise peak location tracks the parameter count (∝d²) of the attention reduction, even in nonlinear Transformers.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: Some theoretical derivations rely on non-rigorous random-matrix heuristics. The full-Transformer experiments use d = 20, 40, 80 and report 10-run averages; the paper notes deviations near the peak or at large sample counts for some architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying sample-wise test-error results were left out. Figure 5(d)'s interpolation-threshold scaling exponents are omitted because they report threshold location rather than test error. Figures 2–4 and 6 concern context length or task diversity, not the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over training epochs. Training runs to convergence.
No capacity sweep across model classes past an interpolation point.
Peak location is tied to #parameters ≈ #samples on the sample axis only. There is no single effective-complexity measure tested across axes.
Label-noise dependence of the sample-wise peak (ρ fixed at 0.01 in Fig. 1 and Fig. 5). Peak splitting. Elimination under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting against an effective number of parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The theory relies partly on non-rigorous random-matrix heuristics, though simulations match it. Belkin et al. (an original source) is cited as the reference for double descent. The record's V6 limits_scope was changed to supports, because the unshown elimination under optimal tuning is untested rather than contradicted. The tranche was changed from T2 to T3.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweeps and whether test error falls, peaks near the size that fits the training set, then falls again.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The study tests pretraining sample count in its synthetic linear-regression setting; it does not establish the result for other tasks or data regimes.
No capacity sweep across model classes tests whether risk improves past an interpolation point.
The study proposes scaling relations for sample count, context length, and task diversity, but does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.

The study reports that stronger ridge regularization suppresses the sample-wise peak. It does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether an optimally tuned regularizer eliminates it.
No re-counting of complexity against an effective number of parameters is tested.
